whyThisMatters: Crewing offers, payslips, and reference-check forms are routine work for HR — which is exactly why attackers copy them so closely. A slightly different domain or an attachment that needs "Enable Content" can hide inside a message that otherwise looks like any other day's work. Today you will build the habit of checking the sender's exact domain and the file type before you open or act on anything that touches pay or a candidate's details.
rememberThis: A professional-looking offer letter, payslip, or reference form is not proof by itself. STOP before opening an attachment or updating any bank or candidate detail — VERIFY the sender's exact domain and, for anything financial, through the portal you already use — then REPORT anything that doesn't match.

discussionPrompts: Ask which detail people noticed first on the spear-phishing card — the sender's exact domain, or did the personal name and real detail make them skip that check?
For the fake login portal, ask how many people actually check the address bar before typing a password on a page that already looks exactly right.
For the QR-code notice, ask who has ever scanned a printed code without checking where it led afterward — what would make that habit stick?
Ask why a 'confidential, don't discuss' instruction from a senior title is the actual warning sign, not a reason to comply faster.
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: People most often miss the spear-phishing and fake-login-portal cards, because a real name/detail or an exact visual copy both feel like proof on their own. The habit to build is the same one used everywhere else: check the exact sending domain or address bar letter by letter — personalisation, visual accuracy, and seniority are all things attackers can fake, none of them are the actual proof.

items.title: Real vs Fake Crewing Offer Email
items.whatIsWrong: The fake Crewing email comes from hr@synergymarine-group-careers.com — it adds a hyphen and the word "-careers". The real address is hr@synergymarinegroup.com. The subject line, logo, and body look almost identical — only the sender address is different.
items.whyItsSuspicious: Crewing teams email people they have never met, so a small change in the address is easy to miss when you are working fast. This check is about reading the sender address letter by letter, not the message body. A fake offer letter with an extra word in the address is a common trick. Always check that the address ends with exactly synergymarinegroup.com — no hyphens or added words. If you are not sure, call the known HR crewing number you already have; do not reply to the address in the email.

items.title: Real vs Fake Payslip & Roster Email
items.whatIsWrong: The fake HR Payroll email has unexpected attachments. One is Payslip_March.pdf.exe — the name ends with .exe, which means it is actually an app, not a PDF. The other is a generic Documents.zip with a password "1234" given in the email. It asks you to "Enable Content" or enter the password. The real payslip email has expected files with clear names: Payslip_Feb2025_RajKumar.pdf and Rotation_Roster_MV-Horizon_Feb-Apr.xlsx, with matching icons and sensible file sizes.
items.whyItsSuspicious: HR Payroll often sends payslips and rotation rosters, so fake attachments blend in. Ask yourself: did you expect this file? Does the name and type match what you were waiting for? A payslip should be a PDF; a roster should be a spreadsheet. You should never need to click "Enable Content" or enter a password to open them. Watch for double endings like .pdf.exe, generic ZIP files, or vague subjects like "Updated Payslip — Please Review Immediately." If unsure, call HR Payroll on a known number before you open anything.

items.title: Real vs Fake Payroll Password Reset Email
items.whatIsWrong: The fake email comes from a different domain (synergymarine-payroll.com vs synergymarinegroup.com). It asks for both your password AND bank details through a link, and invents a 24-hour deadline tied to your pay being delayed.
items.whyItsSuspicious: A genuine system migration is announced through the portal itself and known internal channels — it never asks you to re-enter your password and bank details through an emailed link. Threats about pay being delayed are designed to make you act before you check.

items.title: Real vs Fake Reference Check Email
items.whatIsWrong: The fake email comes from a different domain (crew-solutions-asia.net vs crewsolutions-asia.com). Its attachment is a macro-enabled document instead of a plain form, and it pressures you to "Enable Content" immediately because of a Monday start date.
items.whyItsSuspicious: Recruitment routinely receives forms and CVs from agents, so a fake one blends in easily. The check is the same as any attachment: did you expect this exact file, from this exact domain, in this exact format? A reference form should never need "Enable Content" to open.

items.title: Real vs Fake Bank-Details Confirmation Email
items.whatIsWrong: The fake email comes from a different domain (synergy-payroll-update.com vs synergymarinegroup.com). It asks you to reply with your bank account number and IFSC/SWIFT code directly in an email, instead of using the portal, with an invented threat of "payment failure".
items.whyItsSuspicious: Real HR Payroll processes only ever point you to update your own bank details yourself inside the portal — they never ask you to email your account number and IFSC/SWIFT code back to them. Replying with banking details by email is exactly the goal of this scam.

items.title: Real vs Fake Personalized Follow-Up Email
items.whatIsWrong: The fake email comes from a different domain (synergymarine-hr.com vs synergymarinegroup.com). It uses the recipient's real first name and a genuine recent event (a transfer request) to feel personal, then pivots straight to an urgent bank-detail request via a link.
items.whyItsSuspicious: Personalising an email with your real name and a real recent event is called spear-phishing — attackers gather these details from a previous breach, LinkedIn, or a prior compromised account, specifically to lower your guard. A message being personal is not proof it's genuine; the sender's exact domain is still the only real check, and any bank-detail request still needs a callback on a number you already have.

items.title: Real vs Fake HR Self-Service Login Portal
items.whatIsWrong: The fake portal's address is portal.synergymarine-selfservice.com/hr — a different domain from the real portal.synergymarinegroup.com/hr. The login page itself is copied exactly, down to the layout and colours, so only the address bar gives it away.
items.whyItsSuspicious: Attackers can clone an HR portal's look pixel-for-pixel, but they cannot fake the real address shown in your browser's address bar. Always check the address letter by letter before typing your password, and open the portal from a bookmark you saved yourself rather than a link in an email or message.

items.title: Real vs Fake Printed Benefits Enrolment Notice
items.whatIsWrong: The fake notice's QR code has been swapped — a sticker placed over the original — and it leads to synergy-benefits-enrol.net, not the real portal.synergymarinegroup.com/benefits. It also invents a same-day deadline ("closes TODAY") the real notice never had.
items.whyItsSuspicious: A QR code hides its destination until you scan it — you can't press and hold a printed code the way you can a link in an email. This is quishing (QR-code phishing), and it works precisely because people don't apply the same suspicion to a printed code that they would to a link. Always check the address your phone shows before you continue past the scan, and type the known portal address directly when in doubt.

items.title: Real vs Fake HR Director Payroll Instruction
items.whatIsWrong: The fake email comes from a different domain (synergymarine-group.net vs synergymarinegroup.com). It has no reference number tying it to the normal payroll batch process, and it explicitly instructs you to process it personally, outside the usual system, and keep it confidential.
items.whyItsSuspicious: This is a whaling attack — a senior-title email aimed specifically at HR Payroll staff, using seniority and confidentiality as pressure to bypass a normal process, the same pattern as any Business Email Compromise attempt just aimed at payroll instead of Accounts. A genuine payroll change always references the existing batch/approval process; "confidential, don't discuss" is the red flag, not proof of a special exception.
